articles.title_orig: Trump heads to high-stakes China summit
articles.title_zh: Trump heads to high-stakes China summit
articles.content_orig:
Add Axios as your preferred source to
see more of our stories on Google.
Photo illustration: Brendan Lynch. Photos: Getty Images
President Trump's trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin has the makings of an unpredictable spectacle — and that's exactly what has U.S. allies anxious.
Why it matters: Trump's stated goal for the first-ever summit between the nations' three leaders is to start a discussion on nuclear disarmament. But the fear is that he could go off script and take positions on Ukraine or Taiwan that undermine their interests  or appear to side with their chief adversaries, according to several European officials and Western diplomats.
Driving the news: Before leaving for the Philippines on Monday, Trump reiterated that his goal for the summit is to talk about denuclearization — a "tough subject," he said, "because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right?"
Context: Neither China nor Russia was enthusiastic about discussing denuclearization. But China agreed after Russian lobbying. And Putin saw the summit as a chance to lobby Trump on Ukraine.
Behind the scenes: The Trump-Xi-Putin summit was a topic of closed-door talks among European leaders at a meeting in Dublin last week, according to a European diplomat.
The intrigue: European diplomats said U.S. officials tried to downplay the summit and lower expectations about any substantive results.
State of play: On the same day Trump meets with Xi and Putin, his envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are expected to be in Berlin with senior officials from Ukraine, Germany, France, the UK, Italy, Poland, the EU and NATO, according to two sources.
The other side: Witkoff and Kushner also spoke on Monday with Putin's foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov about the next steps in the peace process.

articles.title_orig: AI chip export controls targeting China gain bipartisan momentum after Nvidia scandal
articles.title_zh: AI chip export controls targeting China gain bipartisan momentum after Nvidia scandal
articles.content_orig:
Five days after Nvidia 's Jensen Huang resigned from the company he co-founded 33 years ago under a cloud of scandal, a nervous base of shareholders eagerly awaited Colette Kress' first public appearance as interim CEO.
Following Nvidia's better-than-expected earnings report on Tuesday, Kress offered some relief to Wall Street, at least temporarily, by proclaiming on the call with analysts that customers are still fully onboard and that there's no slippage in demand. She said leadership from Nvidia's most important supplier, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company , visited company offices this week.
"We've engaged with our customers, we've engaged with our suppliers, our partners, they're all 100% behind us," Kress said on the call. "Customers have expressed their support to the business outlook and helping us through that."
While Huang was a singular figure in artificial intelligence with a commanding presence across the globe, Nvidia is still at the center of the AI ecosystem. Customers ranging from hyperscalers and neoclouds to frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic remain in persistent need of its technology and capital.
Nvidia shares climbed almost 5% in extended trading on Tuesday after the chipmaker's better-than-expected earnings and strong guidance. That still leaves the stock in a deep slump after a 24% drop so far this month, driven by broad concerns about a slowdown in the AI buildout, a political handoff in Washington, D.C., and the turmoil at the top of the company.
Despite all those headwinds and what Nvidia called the "unexpected transition" in leadership, the business is still booming. Revenue more than doubled in the latest quarter to $115.84 billion, and Nvidia projects roughly 90% growth in the current period to about $130 billion.
More importantly, Kress said the 70% growth forecast for next year that was offered over the summer is actually too low. Now the projection is 75%. That's for a company that's seen revenue multiply by about 15-fold since the launch of ChatGPT in late 2022.
While Huang is gone, "demand did not leave with him," Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives said in a note after the report.
Kress maintained her optimistic tone in an interview with CNBC's Jim Cramer after the call.
"The most important thing that we have been seeing is continuing growth in terms of the demand that's out there," she said.
Kress also said on the call that Nvidia's stepped-up buybacks, announced in September, are still on track, confirming that the board had added $150 billion to the company's authorization for share repurchases.
It's not all on Kress. The consistent message throughout the earnings call was that Nvidia is preparing for life after Huang.
Harvey Jones, the newly named chair of Nvidia's board, opened by saying that Huang had resigned after "disclosure of personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and cultural norms," the first time the board had given a reason for his removal.
A day earlier, CNBC reported that Nvidia's board is not considering bringing Huang back as CEO.
Kress said on the call that it's "business as usual." In a statement, she said the company's roadmap is "on track," indicating that there haven't been any changes to future chips and systems currently in development. Nvidia said that the Vera Rubin AI system is off to an "extraordinary start," selling $20 billion in the latest quarter.
But Kress did signal a slight change to the company's willingness to backstop certain projects, and said Nvidia is being "disciplined" with how it's thinking about financing startups.
"There's a lot of discussion internally with a lot of the teams on what we think are the best ones that we want to do," Kress told Cramer. "We're going to continue down that path to make sure we choose the right investments for us to work through going forward,"
Plenty of big questions remain.
Nvidia said its quarterly filing would be published in the "coming weeks," whereas it normally lands on the same day as earnings. On the call, neither Kress nor Jones addressed an avalanche of investigations and hearings in Washington looking into allegations that Nvidia was boosting revenue by selling chips to companies that are passthroughs for buyers in China.
China only came up twice during the call. Kress said Nvidia had sold about $2.4 billion worth of approved data center products to China during the quarter, and that Nvidia had stopped selling licensed Hopper chips to China.
Kress also noted that new trade rules released by the U.S. Commerce Department will cut off Chinese access to renting Nvidia chips.
None of that is stunting growth.
"Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us and employees are committed," Kress said when signing off the call. "We've got this."

articles.title_orig: Trump is trying to put the Iran war behind him, but it’s not over
articles.title_zh: Trump is trying to put the Iran war behind him, but it’s not over
articles.content_orig:
Trump against the backdrop of the Strait of Hormuz | Photo: CENTCOM, Reuters, AFP
With the US midterm elections over, President Donald Trump faces a dilemma over how to bring the war with Iran to an end.
The president's advisers have presented three options. The first, championed by Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, calls for targeted strikes against nuclear and ballistic missile facilities rebuilt since the ceasefire, as well as regime targets, including bases belonging to the Basij militia and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, along with civilian infrastructure and oil facilities. The goal is to weaken the regime in the hope that it will collapse.
The second option is a deal with Iran, an effort led by Vice President JD Vance and Steve Witkoff. At this stage, however, Trump's frustration with Iran's intransigence appears to have exhausted his patience for negotiations. He has therefore sent Vance to deal with the fallout from the midterm elections.
The third option is to maintain the blockade of Iranian ports and continue strangling the country's collapsing economy, an approach led by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent.
The blockade of Iranian ports and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping and oil tankers have so far proved successful. A report by the International Energy Agency (IEA) indicates that the oil market is moving into surplus in the final quarter of 2026, while inventories are beginning to recover. Oil prices are gradually declining and have fallen below $100 a barrel.
There is no doubt that the US operation to reopen the strait has succeeded, dealing a severe blow to the Iranians, who have lost the last strategic weapon at their disposal. Iran's economy is collapsing, and the murderous regime of the ayatollahs is struggling to govern the country and provide its people with basic necessities.
Iran's rulers understand that, under the current strategic circumstances, only the possession of nuclear weapons can ensure their survival. They believe a nuclear deterrent would enable them to bring an end to the blockade and sanctions and begin rebuilding the country.
The Trump administration, for its part, understands Iran's motivations. Following his party's defeat in the midterm elections, Trump himself wants to go down in history as the president who prevented Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons and succeeded in toppling its reign of terror.
On the ground, US forces are making considerable efforts to keep the strait open, exposing Navy vessels to attacks by Iranian unmanned aerial vehicles and drones. The operation requires a sustained American military presence in and around the strait, both at sea and in the air.
In this type of conflict, the Iranians employ terrorist tactics that complicate US operations. It is a form of ongoing security warfare that the IDF knows well from its various theaters of operation, requiring substantial manpower and the adaptation of tactics and equipment to changing conditions. Such an operation demands sustained American resolve.
The arrival of the USS Theodore Roosevelt brings the number of US aircraft carriers in the region to three, providing sufficient military power to launch significant strikes across Iran. It seems unlikely that a force of this size will remain in the region for long. At some point, the USS George Washington is expected to return to Japan.
USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) sails with USS George Washington (CVN 73) in the Arabian Sea, Nov. 17. https://t.co/KCP22Iikx1
— U.S. Central Command (@CENTCOM) November 17, 2026
Trump will spend the coming week in Southeast Asia, where he is scheduled to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, before returning to the US toward the end of the week. His return is expected to open a window of roughly two weeks for a possible strike.
Israel would be an integral part of any attack, should one take place, and would even lead some of the strikes.
IDF soldiers and commanders should be sent into battle by a united government capable of leading the country. Israel's complicated political situation will require party leaders to make difficult decisions. A war against Iran, which would likely also involve Hezbollah, should be conducted under the leadership of a national unity government.

articles.title_orig: Trump arrives in Shenzhen, China, where Xi Jinping’s family history runs deep
articles.title_zh: Trump arrives in Shenzhen, China, where Xi Jinping’s family history runs deep
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Chinese President Xi Jinping welcomed President Trump with a rare in-person greeting Wednesday in Shenzhen for the Chinese leg of Trump's Asia trip this week.
The Chinese leader even offered Trump a hug, kicking off a visit expected to be dogged by questions of US changes to semiconductor export controls and the ongoing scandal at Nvidia . Trade talks with China and Canada are also on the agenda.
The greeting came ahead of two closely watched sit-down meetings Thursday between Trump and Xi on economic issues and another with Russian President Vladimir Putin joining the conversation.
Trump landed in Shenzhen at 4:42 p.m. local time on Wednesday to a red carpet welcome ceremony, a military band playing the Star-Spangled Banner, and a military flyover, according to a pool report.
The pomp mirrored Trump's tarmac greeting for Xi in the United States in September.
Trump also met with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum later on Wednesday. Carney posted on X that the leaders discussed efforts to reach a trade deal and "agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact."
The meeting follows significant trade war escalations that erupted between the US and Canada earlier this fall. Recent weeks have seen a new round of talks aimed at reaching a deal to reduce current duties and avert a threatened 50% tariff on Canadian cars, trucks, and auto parts, scheduled to take effect in 2027.
In his own stops ahead of the meeting, Carney announced progress toward lessening trade restrictions with China and Mexico and also claimed that Canada's growing trade relationship with China is not a major concern for Trump.
"We have been making progress," Carney said of talks with the US, but that any deal needs to be "in the interest of Canadians."
Sheinbaum posted a photo of her sitting down with Trump and said it had been "a very good meeting."
During Wednesday's whirlwind series of stops, Trump and Xi joined a group photo as the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) fully kicked off.
Trump crossed paths with Putin at the festivities, shaking hands and exchanging pleasantries with the Russian leader. The president then participated in a banquet before returning to his hotel for the night.
The gathering this week had been set to focus on digital trade and artificial intelligence, but the scandal at Nvidia ( NVDA ) and potential changes to US semiconductor export rules are hanging over it.
The Trump administration published new proposed export limits as Trump departed Washington, a move that was immediately felt in the region .
The rule aims to limit China's ability to access advanced chips that reside in data centers outside its borders. It was authored by the Department of the Treasury and the National Security Council and has now moved one step closer to being enacted.
Trump traveled to China from the Philippines, where he participated in a series of economic meetings and signed a joint statement with Thailand as the two countries look to finalize a trade deal.
This story has been updated with additional developments.
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: Israel launches ground operation in central Gaza, dozens flee
articles.title_zh: Israel launches ground operation in central Gaza, dozens flee
articles.content_orig:
Israeli tanks advanced in an area of ​the central Gaza Strip on Wednesday, witnesses said, and the Israeli military said its forces were targeting Hamas infrastructure outside areas that Israel controls in ⁠the enclave.
Witnesses said some Israeli tanks rolled onto the main Salahudeen road, west of the Yellow Line that marks the boundary of the two-thirds of the Gaza Strip still under Israeli control despite ⁠a ceasefire that has ​lasted more ⁠than a year.
An Israeli airstrike near the army raid killed one person, Palestinian medics said.
The medics ⁠said separate Israeli airstrikes had killed two other people ​earlier ⁠in the day in ‌ Deir al-Balah and Gaza City.
An Israeli military spokesperson told NBC News that the military was carrying out an operation targeting “Hamas infrastructure” west of ‌the Yellow Line in central Gaza ‌and that it had struck a militant in southern Gaza earlier on Wednesday.
The lates confirmed that it was the first ground operation since the U.S. brokered ceasefire came into effect in October 2025 .
The truce halted major fighting in the Israel-Gaza war although it has not stopped Israeli attacks or secured Hamas’ disarmament.
The spokesperson had no immediate comment on other strikes.
Israel, which says Hamas has recently been regrouping and rearming, has stepped up attacks against the Islamist group. Hamas has accused Israel of attempting to derail the U.S.-brokered ceasefire agreement.
Gaza health ‌authorities say at least 1,600 Palestinians have been ​killed since the ceasefire went into effect, while ‌the Israeli military says five Israeli soldiers have been killed.
Palestinian authorities say more ⁠than 74,000 people in Gaza have been killed in the military campaign ‌that Israel ​launched there after Hamas-led fighters killed ‌about 1,200 people in southern ​Israel in an attack on October 7, 2023.
Chantal Da Silva reports on world news for NBC News Digital and is based in London.

articles.title_orig: Dow slides 400 points, Nasdaq seesaws as Nvidia earnings bounce fizzles: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow slides 400 points, Nasdaq seesaws as Nvidia earnings bounce fizzles: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell on Wednesday as Nvidia shares lost momentum following the chipmaker's better-than-expected earnings report.
The 30-stock index shed 459 points, or 0.9%. The S&P 500 traded down 0.2%, while the Nasdaq Composite rose 0.3%.
Shares of Nvidia were more than 2% lower, reversing course from earlier gains after the company's profit and revenue in the third quarter beat analysts' estimates. The company also lifted its revenue guidance for the fiscal year ending January 2028, calling for 75% growth year over year.
The report marked the chipmaker's first since Jensen Huang resigned last week as CEO, a move that came days after he admitted to an affair with a businesswoman alleged to be a Chinese spy. The company's board chair, Harvey Jones, said at the start of the earnings call that the board doesn't intend to bring Huang back as chief executive.
"It's going to be an adjustment, but it's one that the market will work its way through, just as it always has in the past," said Eric Parnell, chief market strategist at Great Valley Advisor Group.
When it comes to the broader artificial intelligence trade, however, Parnell noted that the underlying fundamental challenges, including those related to capital expenditures and debt financing, haven't changed — and might not anytime soon.
"It doesn't take much of a slowdown in earnings growth in the environment that we're in with the AI buildout and the AI spend to take these types of stocks down pretty quickly," he said. "It's this type of volatility that I suspect we're not only going to continue to see but it's likely to increase as we go through 2027 and into 2028."
The Dow was also weighed down by losses in healthcare stocks like UnitedHealth as well as energy name Chevron and industrial giant Caterpillar . UnitedHealth lost 8%, while Chevron and Caterpillar declined more than 3% and nearly 2%, respectively.
On Tuesday, the blue-chip index dropped more than 1%, while the S&P 500 notched its lowest closing level since July 29. The Nasdaq shed almost 1% and touched its lowest level since April during the session.
Looking ahead, traders are awaiting the Federal Open Market Committee's minutes from its October meeting, which will also be out in the afternoon. Federal Reserve policymakers last month decided to keep the overnight funds rate in a range of 3.75% to 4%.
Investors are also looking ahead to a blockbuster initial public offering from Anthropic later this week. The AI giant's shares are expected to be priced above the current range between $70 and $78, multiple sources told CNBC's David Faber on Tuesday.
Energy stocks fell alongside oil prices as investors reacted to last week's rise in U.S. crude and fuel inventories , even though tensions between the U.S. and Iran persist.
Shares of ExxonMobil and Chevron each dropped more than 3%, while others like ConocoPhillips and EOG Resources were down more than 2%.
S&P 500 energy was the worst performing sector during the session, falling nearly 3%.
That's as crude oil prices were lower on the day. U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell more than 4% to $82.19 per barrel. International benchmark Brent crude futures slid more than 2% to $90.83 per barrel.
Target on Wednesday reported its best sales growth in more than five years and beat Wall Street's revenue expectations, the latest signs of its turnaround strategy taking hold.
The retailer said its net sales grew 7.1% during the fiscal third quarter. Comparable sales rose 5.6%, compared with StreetAccount estimates of up 3.8%. That growth was boosted by a 5% increase in comparable traffic, Target added.
″[It's] a healthy sign that guests are responding to our changes and choosing Target more often," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters. Read more .
SpaceX shares are up more than 3% over the last five sessions as of late morning trading Wednesday, while the Nasdaq Composite is down more than 4%. That separation may be a sign of things to come, according to Morgan Stanley.
"As the AI trade diffuses into its next era, we see scope for further decorrelation and a more durable place in investor portfolios," analyst Adam Jonas wrote in a Tuesday note about SpaceX shares.
Two key things lead Jonas to this prediction: revenue from the company's connectivity — Starlink — vertical, the increasing need for SpaceX's Terafab as the U.S. seeks to create a more independent semiconductor supply chain.
However, a merger between SpaceX and Tesla, Elon Musk's other megacap company, creates a ceiling for the former's stock for now, he said. "Most investors we speak with are broadly comfortable with the merits of a potential combination," Jonas wrote, "but put off by the lack of certainty on timing and potential dilution risk."
Anthropic proxies gained ahead of the company's IPO. Here are some of the moves:
Shares of Amazon and Alphabet rallied 2% and nearly 1%, respectively. The two companies are direct proxies for Anthropic, given their independent investments in the AI company. In April, Amazon agreed to invest up to $25 billion in the company. That same month, Google said it plans to invest up to $40 billion in Anthropic , expanding on a longstanding partnership between the two companies.
Broadcom jumped almost 3%. The chipmaker is a major partner of Anthropic, having announced a special purpose vehicle to finance $63 billion in chips and networking products to be leased to Anthropic.
Retail investor Dan Shetty is so eager to get in on the Anthropic initial public offering that he "drained" his Roth IRA and moved roughly $12,000 from Fidelity to Robinhood for a chance to participate.
"I don't want to tell my grandkids that I didn't invest in Anthropic and I didn't invest in OpenAI during the AI bubble," he said.
Shetty's enthusiasm is shared by many, with excitement among small investors for the blockbuster IPO expected to be off the charts. Vanda Research estimates that Anthropic could see approximately $250 million of retail net buying when it starts trading Thursday, double the size of SpaceX's IPO.
"That would be far and away the largest amount of net retail buying of any stock that we've seen in our data on the first day of its listing," Jai Malhi, senior strategist at Vanda, said in an interview with CNBC.
Read the full story here .
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite began Wednesday's session in the green.
The broad market index climbed 0.2% just after the opening bell, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq moved up 0.6%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 216 points, or 0.4%.
Check out CNBC's live blog here to read more about the stocks making moves before the bell.
— Davis Giangiulio and Fred Imbert
Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller on Wednesday called for aggressive action against inflation, which he said has been more persistent than he expected.
In the near term, the policymaker told CNBC in a live interview that a half-percentage-point increase in the Fed's benchmark rate is probably necessary at the Dec. 8-9 meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee.
From here, he said the Fed needs to reverse the three quarter-point reductions from last year and may need to do more.
"You might need to, like, shock people," Waller told CNBC's Steve Liesman during the "Squawk Box" interview.

The recent crypto sell-off has led Citi to trim its targets for bitcoin and ether.
"We revise our base-case price targets for BTC and ETH to $99,532 and $2,838, respectively, as crypto's holding pattern has broken to the downside, with both assets down since our last update. BTC's break below its 200-day moving average prompts us to cut our near-term flow outlook to neutral," wrote strategist Alex Saunders. articles.title_orig: Stock Market Today: Dow Falls as Nvidia Earnings Fail to Soothe Investors' Nerves
articles.title_zh: Stock Market Today: Dow Falls as Nvidia Earnings Fail to Soothe Investors' Nerves
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia’s leadership sought to set a path forward on Tuesday’s earnings call in the wake of former CEO Jensen Huang’s departure — defying calls to re-hire him, reassuring investors that demand for Nvidia’s products remains strong, and indicating that the leadership shakeup could prompt a new or more cautious approach to key elements of the company’s business.
The company has been rocked by scandal, national security concerns and the resignation of Huang, its founder and CEO of 33 years. And leadership was under pressure to reassure nervous investors Tuesday evening, with Nvidia having lost $751 billion in market value since last Sunday.
Many lingering questions remain. But investors appeared at least somewhat mollified by the comments and earnings results: shares ticked up nearly 5% in after-hours trading following the call.
Nvidia rules out Jensen Huang’s return as CEO, tells investors ‘we’ve got this’
Nvidia Board Chair Harvey Jones kicked off the earnings call by saying the board does not intend to reinstate Huang as CEO, despite Huang’s statement earlier Tuesday that he would be “honored” to return should the board allow it.
Jones said the board has “every confidence” in CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress to lead the company as it searches for a permanent replacement. He added the board wants to install a permanent CEO “as quickly as possible,” but it wouldn’t rush to appoint someone until it finds “exactly the right person.”
The board is considering internal and external candidates for the role. And while Jones offered no further hints on who is under consideration, Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing, joined Kress to take analyst questions on the call — a signal of his importance as a senior leader at the company.
Jones indicated that the board is taking the national security concerns into consideration in its search.
“The board appreciates that we’re living in a world where the advanced silicon technologies and national security dynamics are making major changes in our marketplace,” Jones said. “Our new CEO will have to navigate those waters very carefully.”
Why crisis at NVIDIA reverberates across the AI industry
Nvidia has played a key role in fueling the growth of the AI ecosystem by providing financing and investment to its customers to purchase its chips and build AI infrastructure.
Some industry analysts have questioned whether that will continue without Huang, who was considered the industry’s master dealmaker, even as others criticized the practice as “circular financing” that has artificially inflated the market.
Kress said on the call that the company has committed more than $100 billion to such deals as of the end of the quarter ended in October. However, she indicated that the company will carefully evaluate any deals to back would-be customers going forward.
“We remain thoughtful in how we participate and disciplined in how we commit capital,” Kress said. “We are proud of the role that we have played so far in supporting the ecosystem. As the market matures and additional sources of capital become available, we are rigorously evaluating future investments, commitments, and guarantees.”
Beyond its existing deals, Nvidia will take “a very strong look in terms of the types of companies that we would want to help in terms of the financing,” she said.
The company earned $2.4 billion in sales of licensed chips to China during the third quarter — comprising just over 2% of the total revenue in its core data center business unit. But the company has ceased shipments to the country, Kress said during Tuesday’s call.
That news comes as the company faces increased scrutiny from US officials over the potential illicit transfer of its chips to China.
How the Nvidia scandal lifted the curtain on a loophole that’s giving China access to US chips
A complex network of loopholes of shell corporations and unauthorized brokers, often operating via countries like Singapore, are believed to have enabled the transfer of millions of Nvidia chips to China in violation of export controls. Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., estimated that China and Hong Kong “could comprise roughly 15%” of Nvidia’s previous revenues “when considering potential loopholes throughout Asia.”
The Commerce Department on Monday announced tighter export restrictions to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips via data centers in third-party countries.
The company is assuming no revenue from sales of licensed chips to China in the fourth quarter.
Even prior to Huang’s exit, questions were swirling about whether major tech companies might pull back on their spending on AI infrastructure as they face scrutiny from investors over when the technology will produce meaningful returns.
But Kress said demand for Nvidia’s products continues to outstrip supply, especially as a growing slate of companies and consumers seek to implement computing-intensive AI agents .
“Even in the last week, the continued ask is: How are we going to receive more and more supply to help (customers) with the demand that they have in front of them,” Kress said.
That growing demand pushed the company’s projection for full-year revenue growth in 2028 to 75%, up from its earlier projection of 70%. Nvidia also reported better-than-expected guidance for sales in the final quarter of this year.
“We’ve engaged with our customers, we’ve engaged with our suppliers, our partners,” following Huang’s resignation, Kress said. “They’re all 100% behind us.”

articles.title_orig: Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war
articles.title_zh: Inside the old gas pipeline where Ukraine is fighting an underground war
articles.content_orig:
There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.
For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.
With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line – and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.
Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.
"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."
The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground – accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.
Arriving at the tunnel entrance, the first thing to hit you is the lingering smell of gas and fetid air.
Both sides use openings in the pipeline to get to the surface, where most of the fighting takes place. They have made breaches in the ground, and used welding tools to break through the thick steel.
The Russians were the first to exploit the pipe to infiltrate the nearby city of Kupyansk in September 2025. They have used underground pipelines before, during the capture of the city of Avdiivka in 2024, and last year in their bid to recapture areas of Russia's Kursk region.
But Ukrainian forces have slowly turned the tables.
A specially designed electric cart transports troops and supplies through the pipeline.
They call it the Kupyansk metro. It occasionally breaks down. We travelled on it for 40 minutes, heads bowed and legs crossed. There is a regular bump as you cross the welded sections of the pipe. It is like an austere fairground ride, without the fun.
Our destination was a break in the pipeline where Ukrainian troops have built dug-outs to store ammunition and equipment, with just enough room to stand. It is where the man they call Musician conducts the movement of troops and supplies. He has been living like a mole, his face engrained with dirt and earth.
Musician tells me he has spent the past three months there, with a few brief visits above ground to clean up or go to the toilet. From time to time we can hear the thuds of artillery rounds above. Musician tells me we are close to the line of contact: "But it's safe underground."
The cart continues its journey into the bowels of the earth. It returns about half an hour later with more troops covered in dirt. They have been fighting in positions on the surface.
There is a look of relief on their dust-caked faces.
"It's more comfortable in the pipe because drones don't fly here, and neither do artillery shells or glide bombs," says Vovochka, who has been fighting on the ground for the past three weeks.
But there has been fighting in the pipeline, too. Operation Veles, named after a mythical Slavic god of the underworld, began in April. Since then Ukraine has advanced 15km (9.3 miles) along the pipeline.
It has been painstaking, backbreaking work – with the ever-present fear of coming into contact with the enemy.
Back above ground we meet a few of the soldiers, from the 13th Khartiia Brigade of Ukraine's National Guard, who have taken part in the mission. Their first task was to clear the detritus, water and Russian barricades inside the pipeline.
The Ukrainian troops say some of the barriers were boobytrapped or piled with Russian bodies. "When we moved them or climbed over them, we had no idea what was underneath," says Chyzh.
The other danger, he said, was the ricochets from gunfire when they tried to advance. "You never know where a bullet is going to go or how it will bounce."
His comrade Kort says "we were all firing, we were pushing them back". Over the course of the operation Ukraine says it killed more than 100 Russian soldiers and took 30 prisoners. "Yes, there were bodies," says Kort. "I even had to sleep right next to them."
Their commander's former life as a miner helped prepare them for the physical and psychological challenges of operating underground.
From a building on the surface, Biashym keeps in regular contact with his men still in the pipeline. Behind him is a cabinet full of medicine.
Soldiers in the pipeline spend much of their time on their knees and suffer abrasions. Biashym admits some have had panic attacks from living in such a confined space. Others have struggled to breathe.
Hundreds of Colombian volunteers have also been involved in the operation, part of the RUG 23rd Assault Regiment.
Foreign fighters have helped boost Ukraine's depleted ranks. One of the Colombians, whose call sign is Gecko, tells me it took them 30 days to just clear 500m.
"It was difficult, it was hot and I had fear inside the pipe," he said. "But at some point I just thought, OK, just deal with it and let's advance."
The battle of the pipeline is not over.
Russian forces, like Ukraine's, have built fortified positions inside the pipeline. They still try to infiltrate Ukrainian positions, burrowing their way in and out of the pipe. From a control room above ground we watched Ukrainian drones target another Russian attempt to outflank them.
While some of the fighting taking place underground, there are still battles on the surface and in the air. It has been a combined operation.
But, Zanuda believes it is the best way to fight in the future. "Ground operations are now nearly impossible," he said, adding that "everyone understands, for now, the only way to fight is underground".
There'll be more missions like this, he believes. "Pipelines run everywhere," he said. "You have to remember, back in the Soviet times, oil, gas and ammonia were being transported to Europe, with the entire transit route running through Ukraine."
In reality it has been brutal, gruelling and dangerous work in the harshest of conditions.
It has taken Ukraine seven months to clear 15km of the pipeline.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has hailed it as a success.
It has helped retake lost territory and been a boost for morale, but on its own it has not changed the course of the war.
Additional reporting by Moose Campbell, Volodymyr Lozhko and Rebecca Hartmann

The failure of a Vulcan Centaur rocket carrying a full load of internet satellites for Amazon was caused by an anomaly in its first-stage booster, rocket maker United Launch Alliance said today (Nov. 17).
That failure — which led to the loss of 40 Amazon Leo internet satellites — was recognized about 10 minutes after liftoff, but the problems began much earlier than that, ULA said in a statement.
"While we appear to have lost telemetry and the mission at approximately 10 minutes into flight, early indications are that just after liftoff the launch vehicle experienced low booster performance, resulting in stage separation occurring when the vehicle was low in altitude and below minimal velocity to reach orbit," ULA wrote in today's update .
The two-stage Vulcan Centaur is the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket, which will retire after just six more flights. Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and now has a total of five launches under its belt.
The new rocket has experienced problems on three of those missions. On both its second and fourth flights — which launched in October 2024 and February of this year, respectively — the nozzle of one of Vulcan's strap-on solid rocket boosters (SRBs) fell off about 30 seconds after liftoff.
On both occasions, the rocket overcame the problem and successfully delivered its payloads to orbit. However, after the second occurrence, the U.S. Space Force paused national-security launches with Vulcan until ULA addressed the SRB nozzle issue. (The February 2026 flight was a Space Force mission.)
That work led to "design and process improvements to the nozzle," ULA said in an Oct. 28 update . And those tweaks apparently worked.
"All indications are that the solid rocket booster performance was nominal, following nozzle improvements implemented for this launch," the company wrote in today's update.
Vulcan's Centaur V upper stage, which features two RL-10C engines, did its job as well "but was unable to recover from the [booster] performance loss, resulting in loss of mission," ULA added.
Vulcan's first-stage booster is powered by two BE-4 engines, which are built by Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin . Today's update did not identify the exact problem with the booster; doing so will require more time, as the investigation has just begun.
If that investigation finds a serious issue with the BE-4, there could be broad ripple effects across the American space program. After all, that engine also powers the first stage of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket, which is a key piece of hardware for NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. (And New Glenn is currently recovering from a failure of its own — a massive explosion on the test stand that occurred on May 28 .)
NASA plans to integrate the Centaur V upper stage into its Space Launch System moon rocket, the vehicle that launches Artemis astronauts to space. So the fact that the Centaur performed nominally on Sunday is a bit of good news for the space agency.
Vulcan's grounding is a big deal, no matter what the anomaly investigation ends up finding. The U.S. doesn't have a surfeit of powerful rockets, after all, and two of them — Vulcan and New Glenn — are out of commission at the moment.
There's considerable pressure on both Vulcan and New Glenn to bounce back strong, for the nation faces an impending launch crunch in the next few years. SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy rockets and shift its launch load over to the fully reusable Starship megarocket. SpaceX is expected to prioritize its own needs in Starship's early days, using the vehicle primarily to build out its next-gen Starlink broadband constellation and Starmind AI data center network.
The Vulcan failure also impacts Amazon — specifically, the company's plan to build out Amazon Leo, which will compete with SpaceX's Starlink. Amazon has booked about 100 launches on a variety of rockets to build its constellation, which will eventually consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Thirty-eight of those bookings are for Vulcan; Sunday's launch was the first of those.
The other rockets Amazon has booked are the Atlas V, New Glenn, Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6 . About 400 operational Amazon Leo satellites have reached orbit to date across 14 launches (not including Sunday's failure).
Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

articles.title_orig: Trump plans to meet separately with Putin on his China trip in addition to their 3-way talks with Xi
articles.title_zh: Trump plans to meet separately with Putin on his China trip in addition to their 3-way talks with Xi
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump greets as China's President Xi Jinping welcomes him after Trump steps off Air Force One at Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport in Shenzhen in southern China's Guangdong Province, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Mark Schiefelbein/AP hide caption
SHENZHEN, China — President Donald Trump landed in China on Wednesday, seeking to reinforce the U.S. status as the world's leading technology power, but a distressing series of technical outages back home has left the administration scrambling to calm the American public.
The issues put the administration on the defensive at a moment when the president wants to project strength and certainty ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
As he began his trip to Asia, Trump initially had been nonchalant about the outages that left people in the United States worried about accessing their email, checking their bank accounts or safely flying on an airplane.
"It's fine," Trump pronounced on Tuesday from the Philippine capital of Manila, suggesting it was all just a consequence of being a nation that is "big and powerful."
But then the outages involving Microsoft, the Federal Aviation Administration, JPMorgan Chase and the National Security Agency's communications network began to overshadow Trump's visit. They raised the specter that artificial intelligence can disrupt daily life, as new cyber vulnerabilities identified require software to be constantly upgraded to fix flaws or other security holes, known as patching, which is supposed to improve how the technology runs.
So at the start of the second day of Trump's trip, Secretary of State Marco Rubio stepped in to reassure Americans on Trump's behalf. He told reporters there was "zero" evidence that the outages are connected or tied to rival nations, cyber hackers or criminals.
"Sometimes when you are going in to fix your system because you've identified a vulnerability, it creates a short-term disruption," said Rubio, who is also Trump's national security adviser.
Xi paid Trump a special honor by greeting him on the tarmac after Air Force One arrived in Shenzhen, China, reciprocating a gesture made by the U.S. president during Xi's state visit to Washington in September.
The two leaders greeted each other at the foot of the airplane's stairs in a handshake that became a hug as group of dancers waved flowers and flags. When Putin arrived earlier on Wednesday, Xi did not greet him at the airport despite their longstanding friendship.
Trump has signaled that he wants to take an improvised approach during his time in Shenzhen, the skyscraper-filled tech hub that is hosting world leaders for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. It's a bet that his unscripted brand of diplomacy based on personal relationships can create some kind of legacy to reshape world affairs during his final two years in the White House.
On Thursday, at a first-ever trilateral, Trump said he plans to talk with Xi and Putin about limiting nuclear weapons and bringing an end to the war in Ukraine, which began in 2022 with Russia's invasion. Analysts are not expecting substantive breakthroughs, despite the unprecedented nature of the meeting.
Before the trip, Trump's aides had told reporters that the war in Ukraine would not be on the agenda. But Trump said on Tuesday that the deaths of tens of thousands of Russian troops every month had created an opening to resolve the conflict.
"I think it's very close to getting it done," Trump said. "We're going to have a good meeting on that."
Trump also teased the possibility of a private meeting with Putin and a separate sit-down with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Rubio clarified on Wednesday that Trump was "serious" about meeting with Kim as a way of resolving tensions with North Korea. But he suggested no meeting was currently scheduled between Trump and Kim for Thursday.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., left, walks beside U.S. President Donald Trump during a welcome ceremony marking Trump's state visit to the Philippines at Malacanang Palace in Manila, Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Aaron Favila/AP hide caption
Before he landed in Shenzhen, Trump had lunch in Manila with President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the Malacañang Presidential Palace.
Marcos noted that he had sent fried chicken from the Philippine chain Jollibee to the U.S. delegation for a late-night snack Tuesday and complimented Trump for "working very hard."
Trump praised the U.S. bond with the Philippines and the interior decoration of the presidential palace.
"Our people share common history, common values, common interests, common architectural tastes," Trump said. "I love what you've done here."
He said after their meeting that the two nations had reached a trade deal on Wednesday, though he had also said last year that an agreement had been reached. The U.S. trade deficit in goods with the Philippines has risen under Trump, climbing from $4.9 billion in 2024 to $12.8 billion during the first 9 months of this year, according to the Census Bureau.
There were no details about the new agreement, although the White House said it will involve Manila buying more energy and farm products.
Trump also had a short reunion with Imelda Marcos, the former first lady and mother of the Philippines' current president.
Famed for her lavish shoe collection, Imelda Marcos knew Trump decades ago through the New York City party scene. During the 1986 "People Power" uprising, her husband, Ferdinand Marcos, was ousted as the Philippines' strongman leader.
Trump called her "always the most beautiful" and the 97-year-old matriarch appeared to hand him a gift, according to a video posted by the White House.
Russian President Vladimir Putin speaks at the APEC CEO summit held ahead of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, southern China's Guangdong province on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026. Dmitry Azarov/Pool Sputnik Kremlin hide caption
The prospect of Trump meeting with two of America's largest geopolitical rivals has been a source of unease as the U.S. president has been less welcoming of historic allies such as Canada and NATO partners in Europe.
His tariffs that were intended to curb China's trade surplus have done little to stop the progress of the world's dominant manufacturer, which for the second straight year will have exported $1 trillion more in goods than what it imported.
Even without the digital outages in the U.S., questions about how to handle AI loom over the summit.
The technology is viewed as key to unlocking faster economic growth, but its rapid development has meant it poses national security risks and could evolve in ways that put AI beyond human control.
Trump's close tech industry ally Jensen Huang was recently removed as the CEO of Nvidia after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged to be an agent of the Chinese government. Beijing has denied that she was a spy, yet the affair raised concerns about how China has been able to access Nvidia computer chips to develop its own AI models that are competing with the U.S.
When asked this week why the U.S. had not been more aggressive in cutting off China's access to advanced computer chips, Trump said there were differences of opinion inside his administration and that "We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them."
Trump has said he does not plan to bring up Taiwan, a self-governing island that China claims as its own. Taiwan is the leading manufacturer of advanced computer chips, including those designed by U.S. companies.
Still, Trump expects that Xi will push him on Taiwan's sovereignty.
"I'm sure he'll raise it," Trump said. "I won't have to raise it."

articles.title_orig: Trump Says the U.S. Will “Catch” China on Rare Earths Within 10 Months - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.title_zh: Trump Says the U.S. Will “Catch” China on Rare Earths Within 10 Months - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.content_orig:
SHENZHEN, China — In a rare and surprising move, Chinese leader Xi Jinping personally greeted President Donald Trump as he arrived in China on Wednesday ahead of historic three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin .
It is believed to be the first time that Xi, in power for more than a decade, has been on hand to greet any foreign leader arriving in China.
He was reciprocating the personal greeting he had received from Trump in September, when the American leader met him at the plane upon his arrival for a White House state visit . Lawmakers from both parties had criticized Trump over the move, which is also rare for U.S. presidents.
A report by Xinhua, China’s state-run news agency, said that during Trump’s arrival in the city of Shenzhen on Wednesday, Xi noted the special trip the American president and first lady Melania Trump had made to welcome him at Joint Base Andrews outside Washington.
“China is a nation that values courtesy and has a tradition of returning goodwill with goodwill,” the Xinhua report said.
After Trump descended from Air Force One, a handshake between the two leaders turned into a quick hug as rows of military regiments and performers wearing bright pink and turquoise outfits stood at attention. A martial band played the American and Chinese national anthems as dancers waved flowers, pompoms and Chinese and American flags.
Xi’s gesture Wednesday most likely reflects a desire by him and his government to “show respect to Trump,” which they know he enjoys, William Yang, a senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group, said in a post on X .
“It is likely also an attempt to uphold the positive rapport between Xi and Trump ahead of a potentially turbulent period in U.S.-China relations in the coming months,” he said.
When Trump last visited China in May, he was greeted at the airport in Beijing by Vice President Han Zheng.
Putin, who has a close relationship with Xi and has met with him 50 times as of Wednesday, did not receive a personal greeting from the Chinese leader when he arrived earlier at Shenzhen Bao’an International Airport. Putin was instead met by Cai Qi, a close Xi adviser and member of the Politburo Standing Committee.
Xi has met with a number of world leaders, including Putin, as they gather in Shenzhen this week for a summit of Asia-Pacific economies.
Trump, Putin and Xi are holding an unprecedented trilateral meeting Thursday on the sidelines of the summit.
Ahead of his bilateral meeting with Xi on Wednesday, Putin said he expected “great potential benefits” from the trilateral talks, which have sparked anxiety in places such as Ukraine, Iran and the Beijing-claimed island of Taiwan, where officials worry the world’s three most powerful leaders could make decisions about their futures without consulting them.
In a briefing last week, a senior U.S. official said the trilateral meeting was unlikely to produce any sort of agreement, describing it as an “entry point” and “the first conversation.”
Jennifer Jett is the Asia Digital Editor for NBC News, based in Hong Kong.
Erin Tan is a news researcher in NBC News’s Beijing bureau.

articles.title_orig: ‘GTA VI’ Nears $1.7 Billion In Pre-Order Sales—One Day Before Launch
articles.title_zh: ‘GTA VI’ Nears $1.7 Billion In Pre-Order Sales—One Day Before Launch
articles.content_orig:
The review embargo on “Grand Theft Auto VI” has finally lifted and the game, which on Tuesday was nominated for Game of the Year ahead of its launch, is considered Rockstar Games’ latest masterpiece.
“ GTA 6 ” currently holds a score of 99 on Metacritic , which ties it with the original 1998 Nintendo 64 version of “The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time” for the highest-rated video game of all time on the platform. (The recently released remake of “Ocarina of Time” for Switch 2 has a score of 96 on Metacritic and is also a 2026 Game of the Year contender.)
“Many superlatives will be heard in the discussion around ‘ Grand Theft Auto VI ‘ – biggest world, most activities, best graphics, deepest narrative – but its real triumph is the way all those features and others work in service of a cohesive, believable immersion in a criminal fantasy that is hard to grasp until you’ve played it for yourself,” Game Informer’s Matt Miller wrote in his review, which gave the game a perfect score of 10.
Thirteen years in the making , “GTA 6” is a massive open-world game that follows protagonists Jason Duval and Lucia Camino (voiced by Manni L. Perez) who find themselves stuck in the midst of a criminal conspiracy in the fictional state of Leonida after a score goes wrong.
“Jason Duval and Lucia Caminos are an interesting pair of playable characters, and unlike any leads that have come before them in the series,” Luke Reilly wrote for IGN . “Their motivations and goals are very different from the main characters of previous ‘GTA’ games, and their priority is really about escape rather than revenge or empire building. They’re not angels, and it is invariably their recklessness as small-time crooks that puts them in the wrong place at the wrong time, but the overall sliminess of their far more powerful antagonists does make the couple easy to root for throughout their story – which unfolds like four or five seasons of a prestige TV show.”
“GTA 6” officially launches Thursday in the U.S. but has begun rolling out worldwide as the clock strikes midnight on Nov. 19 in different territories, starting with New Zealand, which got access to the game Wednesday at 6 a.m. ET. While fans had been waiting to see if and when “GTA 6” reviews would drop before the game did (with several debating The Game Awards nominations being revealed before “GTA 6” was out), Rockstar Games chose to set the embargo in line with the game’s public release.
The game costs $80 for the standard edition and $100 for the ultimate version and reportedly offers approximately 80 hours of gameplay to complete its main storyline alone.
“Leonida is so lifelike that at times it beggars belief, so vast that it feels overwhelming, and outside the story missions you can do whatever you please,” The Guardian’s Keza MacDonald wrote . “There are nightclubs, gyms, flea markets, malls, restaurants, clothes shops, basketball courts, shooting ranges, aircraft hangars, projects and mansions, places to hunt and fish or go kayaking, gas stations and thousands of individuals engaged in conversation as you pass by. Interesting things are always happening in your peripheral vision. You might witness the cops chasing someone down to plant drugs on them, or overhear an interesting confrontation, or see a car speeding away and wonder where it’s going – though interesting things always seemed to happen when I was driving a stolen car at high speed towards a discerning buyer, or otherwise unable to stop and follow my nose. Thankfully, another opportunity would always present itself.”
“I have quibbles about some clunky controls and some story pacing problems in the game’s later chapters, but like crappy cupholders in a million-dollar supercar, they don’t really get in the way of what’s here. Instead, they’re minor issues to point at as I hit the gas and go 200 MPH with the radio blasting,” Kotaku’s Zack Zwiezen wrote .

articles.title_orig: Iran attacks US air base in Kuwait
articles.title_zh: Iran attacks US air base in Kuwait
articles.content_orig:
Iran has launched new attacks on its Gulf neighbours, targeting an airbase used by the United States military in Kuwait and carrying out several attacks on Bahrain after the US bombed Iran’s Qeshm Island.
Kuwait said it activated its air defences to counter drone strikes – the first since early September – and Bahrain said it fended off an Iranian attack early on Wednesday, a day after the US attacked a missile launch site on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz.
The US said it carried out the strike in response to an Iranian attack on a US radar installation in Bahrain earlier on Tuesday.
Bahrain, which hosts the US Navy’s 5th Fleet, has experienced four Iranian attacks in six days, ending a weeks-long respite in the war that started with US-Israeli strikes on Iran on February 28.
Iran said its recent attacks were in response to US drone surveillance operations and an attack on Iranian communications towers.
The uptick in fighting raises the risk of a wider escalation towards the resumption of all-out conflict nearly nine months into the war, and complicates negotiations for a diplomatic solution, which have stagnated despite intensified mediation efforts from Qatar.
The Iranian attacks on the Gulf countries have drawn condemnation from across the region.
Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs condemned the Iranian attacks on Kuwait and Bahrain “in the strongest terms” and denounced an attack on a tanker belonging to the United Arab Emirates.
The ministry said the kingdom rejects Iran’s disruption of shipping routes and urged a negotiated solution.
Arab League chief Nabil Fahmy said the repeated attacks on Arab countries reveal “a continuous escalation pattern that threatens to widen the circle of confrontation”. He also condemned the targeting of a ship belonging to the UAE’s national oil company, ADNOC, as it crossed the Strait of Hormuz.
Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, the Gulf Cooperation Council’s secretary-general, held Iran “responsible for this escalation and its repercussions on regional security”.
Qatar’s Foreign Ministry called the attacks “a dangerous escalation” that risks undermining diplomatic efforts. Kuwait and the UAE also condemned them.
Kuwait’s Foreign Ministry described the drone attacks as flagrant violations of its sovereignty and a direct threat to its security, Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi reported from Doha.
Basravi also said Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, Majed al-Ansari, warned that continued escalation without restraint from both the US and Iran makes a negotiated solution, or even continued dialogue, harder.
Meanwhile, Iran’s army chief, Major-General Amir Hatami, said the armed forces were “monitoring the enemy’s movements” after a third US aircraft carrier arrived in the Middle East, the Fars news agency reported.
He said Iran’s response to any misstep by the US and its “backers” would be “even more crushing”.

articles.title_orig: Mexico Leader Goes Viral in China for 21-Hour Economy Flight
articles.title_zh: Mexico Leader Goes Viral in China for 21-Hour Economy Flight
articles.content_orig:
President Claudia Sheinbaum promoted Mexico as an investment destination in an address to the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit in Shenzhen, China, on Tuesday.
In a 13-minute speech , she also touted Plan México — the federal government’s overarching economic and industrial policy — and spoke about a range of initiatives and achievements of her two-year-old administration.
Desde Shenzhen, China, les comparto mi participación en APEC CEO Summit 2026; en representación de México, expusimos a líderes económicos y empresarios del mundo que el desarrollo con bienestar es posible. https://t.co/3AEDA9Wve3
— Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) November 17, 2026
According to a Xinhua news agency article posted to a Chinese government website , the APEC CEO Summit 2026 brings together “business and political leaders from across the Asia-Pacific and beyond to discuss regional economic cooperation and future development.”
“Under the theme ‘To Prosper and Win the Future Together,’ the two-day event has attracted more than 2,000 representatives from 21 APEC economies and 13 non-APEC economies, including Britain, France, Germany and Switzerland,” the article says.
“Participants include representatives from 115 Fortune Global 500 companies, as well as heads of several international organizations and representatives of business associations from Russia, the United States and other economies.”
In addition to speaking at the APEC CEO Summit, Sheinbaum will attend the APEC Leaders’ Meeting during her visit to Shenzhen. She arrived in the southern Chinese city on Monday and is scheduled to return to Mexico on Friday.
Promoting Mexico as a destination for foreign investment, Sheinbaum touted Mexican talent as well as the country’s geographic location and its trade agreements with other nations, among other competitive advantages.
“We have engineers. We are among the top five countries in the world in terms of the number of engineers produced. We have public universities, research centers, highly educated young people and a strong industrial tradition,” she said.
“We have the capacity to participate in major global value chains, but also to innovate and build strategic industries. We have a privileged geographic location, an extensive network of trade agreements, an economy integrated into the world’s major markets, natural resources, expanding infrastructure and, above all, the human talent of a hardworking people,” Sheinbaum said.
“Mexico guarantees conditions for investment, certainty and a long-term vision for development,” she said.
As part of Plan México, the federal government is seeking to attract more foreign investment to Mexico and strengthen and support the country’s vast manufacturing sector.
Foreign direct investment in Mexico reached a record high of almost US $35 billion in the first six months of 2026 , but the pace of year-over-year growth, at 2.1%, was not particularly strong.
By speaking at the APEC CEO Summit, Sheinbaum had the opportunity to court investment from major companies in APEC economies and beyond.
Three of Mexico’s five leading sources of foreign investment in the first half of 2026 are APEC members, namely the United States, Canada and Australia. Investment from China has increased in recent years , but the East Asian economic powerhouse was not among the top investors in Mexico last year .
Insecurity, uncertainty surrounding the future of the USMCA free trade pact — which the U.S. government has so far declined to extend to 2042 — and Mexico’s controversial judicial reform, which introduced the popular election of judges , are seen as among the factors discouraging investment in Mexico.
At the start of her address, Sheinbaum highlighted that Mexico is the world’s 11th most populous country and 13th largest economy.
“But above all, we are a nation with a history stretching back thousands of years, where Spanish is spoken, but so are 68 indigenous languages,” she said.
Sheinbaum went on to say that Mexico is building its “own” economic model with “roots in our history, our cultural greatness, and the strength, talent and capabilities of our people.”
“This transformation began in 2018. And starting in 2024, with the election of Mexico’s first female president, we gave it a new dimension through Plan México,” she said.
“Plan México is a vision for the nation. It is the decision to turn our capabilities, resources, strategic position, and talent into drivers of development grounded in sovereignty and social justice,” she said.
She said that the plan is based on “five principles,” namely “shared prosperity; energy and food sovereignty; public, private, and public-private investment in infrastructure; incentives for private investment; and environmental responsibility in the face of climate change.”
Sheinbaum also said that Plan México “has a humanist vision” in which “the economy is at the service of the people” rather than the other way around.
“For decades, it was argued that the wealth of a select few had to grow first, and that over time, the benefits would trickle down to the rest of society. In Mexico, we are proving that the path can be very different,” she said.
Sheinbaum said the government and private companies are expected to invest a total of US $432 billion in infrastructure under Plan México between 2024 and 2030.
“We are transforming the country’s productive capacity, connecting regions, bringing markets closer together, improving logistics, and creating jobs,” she said.
“At the same time, we are promoting investment in industry and services through incentives, certainty, streamlined administrative procedures, and new development hubs aligned with each region’s economic strengths. This has enabled us to become the fifth-largest economy in the world in terms of foreign direct investment,” Sheinbaum said.
In her closing remarks, she said she hadn’t traveled to China “just to offer investment opportunities.”
“We came to share a vision for the future,” she said.
“A vision in which Mexico grows and, at the same time, all economies become stronger and prosperity is a shared achievement,” Sheinbaum said.
In various ways, Sheinbaum’s address at the APEC CEO Summit was similar to her annual government report ( informe ) speeches, the most recent of which she delivered on Sept. 1 . The difference was that her speech in Shenzhen on Tuesday was delivered on the world stage and was directed at international businesspeople and leaders rather than a domestic audience.
In a vast auditorium in China’s tech capital, Sheinbaum acted as cheerleader in chief for Mexico, and also for the fourth transformation (4T) political project she leads. She highlighted that since Andrés Manuel López Obrador — the founder of the 4T — became president eight years ago, Mexico’s minimum wage has increased 154% in real terms and some 17 million people have been lifted out of poverty , according to World Bank data.
Sheinbaum also spoke about Mexico’s various social programs, and declared that her government is establishing a “ verdadero estado de bienestar ” — a phrase that can be read as a “true welfare state” or, more broadly, a country that prioritizes people’s well-being.
In addition, she highlighted her government’s major investment in highway, rail, electricity, water, port and housing projects.
Sheinbaum’s speech to the APEC CEO Summit came a day before Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to address the event. Li Qingshuang , vice-chairperson of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade, said on Sunday that leaders from 12 APEC economies, including Canada, Chile and South Korea, will attend the APEC CEO Summit and deliver speeches or remarks, or participate in panel discussions.

articles.title_orig: 8BitDo Reveals Its Own GameCube Controller For Switch 2
articles.title_zh: 8BitDo Reveals Its Own GameCube Controller For Switch 2
articles.content_orig:
8BitDo, known for its work in providing excellent retro-inspired controllers for modern systems, has announced the GC Bluetooth Gamepad to celebrate the GameCube's 25th anniversary. It's currently scheduled to launch on 10th December 2026 .
Compatible with Switch, Switch 2, and Windows, the GC controller maintains the core shape and layout of the iconic GameCube pad, but adds in a bunch of modern upgrades like TMR sticks and Hall Effect triggers. Priced at $49.99 , it undercuts Nintendo's official offering by $20 and is available for pre-order now.
Colours include purple and orange, which are arguably the most recognisable from the original release (though we're hoping for a Wavebird-inspired silver variant in the future, too). The pad also features single-rotor rumble to replicate the feel of the original, while a new 'ZL' button – which also features on the official Nintendo GameCube pad for Switch 2 – has been designed to be symmetrical to the 'Z' button on the right.
While we do have a dedicated capture button, there unfortunately doesn't appear to be a 'C' button for chat purposes. It's also not clear at this stage whether the GC controller will have wake-up support for Switch 2, but 8BitDo has generally been pretty good at including this, even if it's not necessarily supported immediately at launch.
Here's an official list of features from 8BitDo:
- Classic GC design and iconic button layout - TMR joysticks with octagonal gates - Hall Effect linear triggers - Single-rotor rumble - Symmetrical Z and ZL bumpers - Capture button for screenshots and recording - Turbo function - Support for multiple simultaneous gamepad connections
Finally, it's worth noting that if you purchase the 8BitDo Retro Receiver for GC , you can use the new controller – or indeed the official GameCube pad – with original hardware.

articles.title_orig: Wall Street prepares for Anthropic IPO frenzy, despite broader AI stock slump
articles.title_zh: Wall Street prepares for Anthropic IPO frenzy, despite broader AI stock slump
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic is considering upsizing its initial public offering, people familiar with the details told CNBC, as the artificial intelligence lab weighs setting the price well above $80.
The company closed its order books and locked in total demand on Tuesday, setting the stage for the Claude creator's eagerly awaited Nasdaq listing. Institutional demand for the offering is around $400 billion, while retail demand is approaching $100 billion, according to the people, who asked not to be named because they were not authorized to speak publicly.
The orders are indications of interest and are not binding. All of the details are subject to change, and Anthropic will make final decisions Wednesday afternoon, the people said. Anthropic is expected to set its final IPO price after market close Wednesday.
Demand for the offering is higher than it was for Elon Musk's SpaceX , even though the rocket maker had a bigger market offering. SpaceX debuted on the Nasdaq in June in by far the biggest IPO on record, ultimately raising $85.7 billion.
The AI lab said last week that it would offer 825 million shares in the IPO at a price range of between $70 and $78 per share, which would net up to $64.35 billion at the high end of that range.
A representative for Anthropic declined to comment.
Anthropic's listing is a major test for the AI industry, which has experienced a set of recent shocks, including a dramatic backlash that was felt at the polls in the midterm elections and last week's ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . The market was already jittery on concerns that rising interest rates will make debt unaffordable for many data center developers and neoclouds.
Tech's biggest companies have significant exposure to Anthropic, as an investor, partner or customer. Amazon and Google both own stakes valued at over $100 billion, and a group of tech companies, including Google, Microsoft , Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices agreed to collectively invest $26 billion in the IPO. Anthropic, meanwhile, is a buyer of costly systems from Nvidia, Google, Amazon and AMD.
"I think if we do this right, we can create an age of miracles where humanity is able to solve problems that have eluded us for millennia," Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said in Anthropic's roadshow video . "We have to make sure that all the risks, all the ways that things can go wrong with this technology, we very carefully address those risks as we bring the benefits and as we have a viable business at the same time."
Amodei co-founded Anthropic alongside a handful of other researchers less than six years ago, after the group collectively defected from OpenAI. The company is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , and it primarily sells its products and services to other businesses.
Anthropic has been racing to maintain an edge over OpenAI and Google in the enterprise market, and it experienced a period of explosive growth in 2026, driven largely by the popularity of its AI coding tool, Claude Code. OpenAI has confidentially filed for an IPO and has said a debut is likely in 2027.
For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said, it generated $33.24 billion in revenue, up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year, according to its prospectus. The company reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.
Anthropic said in an amended filing that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month.
The company has faced plenty of challenges during its meteoric rise over its positions on safety, regulation and national security, leading to two high-profile disputes with the U.S. government this year. Its prospectus included more than 90 pages of risk factors for investors to consider ahead of its IPO.
"Our aim is to help humankind chart a safe course through this technological evolution, open new frontiers of discovery, and bring forth an age of miracles," Anthropic's co-founders wrote in the company's prospectus. "Everyone who owns our stock, whether an institution or an individual, becomes part of that effort."
